paragraphs: Irish Rail had a plan for a new computer system. The system would control trains from Heuston Station in Dublin.
A Spanish company called Indra was building it. The plan was to spend about €19 million. But the work was very late and cost too much. In July, Irish Rail ended the contract.
Now Indra wants more than €30 million from Irish Rail. Irish Rail says it owes nothing. It has already lost €50 million on the project. Indra says its system works well in other countries.
Irish Rail wants a new system from Siemens. It should be ready in Dublin by late 2028. The whole country may have it by 2031.
A Spanish technology company wants Irish Rail to pay it more than €30 million for a computer project that has been stopped.

The company, Indra, was building a new traffic management system to control trains across Ireland from Heuston Station in Dublin. The project was first expected to cost about €19 million, but it had years of delays and rising costs. Irish Rail ended the contract on 17 July.

Irish Rail says no money is owed to Indra. It has already written off €50 million that it spent on the system, and it says Indra never delivered a working product. Indra says its system works well in Spain, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Lithuania.
Irish Rail's chief executive, Mary Considine, will speak about the problem to a committee of TDs and senators.

Irish Rail now wants a new system designed by Siemens. It should be mostly ready in the Dublin area by late 2028, and across the country by 2031. The National Transport Authority has not yet approved the plan.
Spanish IT company Indra is seeking more than €30 million from Irish Rail as part of the final accounts for a train traffic management system that has now been scrapped.

The system, based at Heuston Station in Dublin, was meant to control trains across the national network. It was originally expected to cost around €19 million but suffered years of delays and cost overruns, and Irish Rail terminated the contract on 17 July.

Irish Rail rejects Indra's claim, insisting that no money is due. It has already written down €50 million on the investment and is pursuing the financial consequences of what it describes as the lack of a finished product. Indra says its system is successfully in use in Spain, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Lithuania, and it has reserved all its rights.
Chief executive Mary Considine is due to brief the Oireachtas transport committee on the dispute.

Irish Rail now plans to replace the system with one designed by Siemens, to be substantially complete in the Greater Dublin Area by late 2028 and nationwide by 2031. However, the National Transport Authority has yet to approve the national rollout.
Spanish IT firm Indra is pursuing Irish Rail for upwards of €30 million in connection with the final accounts for a train traffic management system that has since been abandoned.

The Heuston-based system was intended to oversee train movements across the entire network. Initially budgeted at roughly €19 million, it became mired in years of delays and spiralling costs, prompting Irish Rail to terminate the contract on 17 July.

Irish Rail flatly rejects the claim, maintaining that nothing is owed. Having already written down €50 million on the venture, it is seeking redress for what it portrays as Indra's failure to deliver a viable product. Indra, for its part, counters that its technology operates successfully in Spain, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Lithuania, and has reserved all its rights.
Chief executive Mary Considine is expected to address the Oireachtas transport committee on the matter.

The company intends to replace the system with a Siemens alternative, which should be substantially complete in the Greater Dublin Area by late 2028 and nationwide by 2031. Crucially, the national rollout still awaits sign-off from the National Transport Authority.

The Spanish IT company Indra is seeking payments potentially exceeding €30 million from Irish Rail in relation to the final accounts for a train traffic management system that has subsequently been discontinued.

The system, located at Heuston Station, was designed to regulate train movements across the national network. Although its initial projected cost was approximately €19 million, the project was characterised by prolonged delays and substantial cost overruns; consequently, Irish Rail terminated the contract on 17 July.

Irish Rail categorically disputes the claim, asserting that no payment is due. Having already written down €50 million on the investment, it is pursuing compensation for what it regards as the absence of a functional product. Indra, conversely, contends that its system has been successfully deployed in Spain, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Lithuania, and it has reserved all its rights.
Chief executive Mary Considine is scheduled to brief the Oireachtas transport committee regarding the dispute.

Irish Rail proposes to replace the system with an alternative designed by Siemens, which is expected to be substantially complete in the Greater Dublin Area by late 2028 and nationally by 2031. Nevertheless, the national implementation remains contingent upon approval from the National Transport Authority.
